note: One entry per rule whose positive case could plausibly also be a TypeScript error. `scripts/tsc-oracle-gate.mjs` asks both sides of that question about the same bytes: it compiles each `code` against the real published typings (fixtures/tsc-oracle/packages.json) and enforces `expect`, and it runs the checker over the same snippet in its own project and enforces `checker`. A case that declared only TypeScript's side could be satisfied by a rule that reports nothing at all, which is why `checker` is required. See docs/precision-backlog.md for the full redundancy ledger, of which this file is the executable part.

expectations.silent: TypeScript must report nothing. The rule's claim is therefore its own. A diagnostic here means the rule now duplicates `tsc` and must be narrowed or deleted -- that is the gate AGENTS.md's absolute rule was missing.
expectations.distinct-claim: TypeScript does report something, but about a different defect than the finding asserts. Requires `allow` (the diagnostic codes seen) and `why` (what the finding claims that the type error does not). Never use this to keep a rule whose claim is the type error's claim.
expectations.removed-because-redundant: TypeScript must report a diagnostic. The rule that used to fire here was deleted for exactly that reason, and this direction is pinned so that a future Solid release which loosens the type -- making `tsc` silent again -- fails this gate and forces the removal to be reconsidered rather than quietly leaving a hole. Requires `checker: "silent"`: the claim is that the checker has already stopped here, and before the gate ran the checker that half was taken on trust -- a case could pin the diagnostic while the rule went on reporting the same expression.
expectations.redundant-pending-narrowing: TypeScript must report a diagnostic, and the checker *also* still reports here -- a known, documented duplicate whose narrowing is specified in docs/precision-backlog.md but not yet landed. Distinct from `removed-because-redundant`, which asserts the checker has already stopped. Use this only with a ledger entry naming the narrowing; it is a debt marker, not a resting place.

checkerExpectations.reports: The exact dialect rule named by `rule` reports on this snippet in strict and loose checker projects, with the declared finding kind. Paired with `expect: "silent"` this is a *keystone*: TypeScript says nothing and the rule still speaks. Every catalog rule needs one or an EXEMPT entry in the gate; checked-in snapshots cannot substitute for executable oracle evidence.
checkerExpectations.silent: The exact dialect rule does not report on this snippet in either checker project. Legitimate for a negative case, for a case pinning a spelling a narrowing deliberately gave up, and for `removed-because-redundant`, where it is required. It is never legitimate as a rule's only declaration: a rule silent on every case has been narrowed into a no-op.

distinctFindings.why: The owner finding asserts that allocated computations at module scope are never disposed; TS2345 only rejects each apply callback's return value.

cases.why: SC3004, removed 2026-08-17. `EffectFunction` returns `(() => void) | void`, so every spelling the rule proved -- contextual, explicit, returned call, member -- is a type error. `(() => void) | void` is a union, not bare `void`, so return-value-ignoring assignability does not rescue it.

The legal spellings the removed rule accepted. Pinned so the removal cannot be re-justified by a type that rejects *everything*: the type draws the same line the rule drew, which is what made the rule redundant rather than merely weaker.

distinctFindings.why: The owner finding asserts that an allocated module-scope computation is never disposed; the type diagnostics concern callback return and argument assignability.

cases.why: SC9002, removed 2026-08-17. The obligation's whole domain was the *legality* of a returned value, and the type system closes legality: a mixed union and an `unknown` return are type errors, and the second argument being a non-callback value at all is a type error.

The rest of SC9002's domain, and the reason narrowing it was not an option. `any` leaves `tsc` silent, but `any` is missing evidence rather than proof of a defect (AGENTS.md). The `{ effect, error }` bundle is a supported API form -- `EffectBundle` -- so the obligation the rule raised there was noise on idiomatic code, not a limit worth reporting.

distinctFindings.why: The reactive-read finding concerns reading a source outside tracking while forming the target; TS2345 concerns whether the resulting value carries the refresh brand.

cases.why: SC7003, removed 2026-08-17. `Refreshable<T> = T & { readonly [$REFRESH]: any }` encodes the source brand *as a type*, so every target shape the rule proved invalid -- a wrapper thunk, a read value, an object literal, a plain accessor, a store child record, and a value-form store -- is TS2345 against it. A valid target type-checks, so the type draws the same line the rule drew.

The valid targets, pinned so the removal cannot be justified by a type that rejects everything. `refresh(memo)` and `refresh(signalGet)` type-check because `createMemo`/`createSignal` return `Refreshable` accessors.

distinctFindings.why: The reactive-read finding concerns invoking an accessor outside tracking; TS2345 concerns passing that returned value as an affects target.

cases.why: SC7004, removed 2026-08-17. A key on an accessor target selects the one-argument `affects(target: Accessor<unknown> | Store<object>)` overload, whose second parameter does not exist, so TypeScript reports TS2345 on the key itself -- exactly the rule's claim.
The legal `affects` forms from the rc.0 doc comment: a bare accessor, a store record, and a record plus one of its own keys.

SC9003, both names, removed 2026-08-17. The obligation asked whether the target carries the source brand, and the brand is a type: an untraceable target is TS2345 and a branded one type-checks, so there was nothing left to be uncertain about.

SC7001 is independent. The single-argument `createEffect(compute)` overload still exists in rc.0 -- deprecated, and typed to return `never` -- so `tsc` accepts the call. The finding's claim is that the effect never runs, which no part of that signature says.

Both calls are accepted because an explicit assertion hides the runtime value from the published effect signature. The first uses TypeScript's angle-bracket assertion syntax, which is legal only in a .ts source; the second hides a non-callable EffectBundle.effect property. Neither assertion changes the runtime value, so both remain proven MISSING_EFFECT_FN failures that TypeScript cannot report.

A parameter may legally shadow the global undefined binding, so this must never be mistaken for the global nullish value or promoted to a violation. The non-null assertion is still a runtime-transparent escape and a loose project cannot prove it redundant, so the exact outcome remains uncertifiable rather than silently certified.

The compiler proves this tuple has two elements, but exact arity does not describe the hidden apply value. The value may be callable or may trigger MISSING_EFFECT_FN, so the checker retains an uncertifiable obligation instead of silently certifying the call.

The compiler proves this required-only tuple has exactly one element. After expansion the Solid 2 apply slot is therefore absent, so the runtime MISSING_EFFECT_FN failure is a violation even though TypeScript accepts the deprecated one-argument overload.

The published overload accepts `any`, but that runtime value may be a callable apply function, a valid effect bundle, or a value that triggers MISSING_EFFECT_FN. With no exact runtime fact, both safety and failure remain possible and must stay explicit.

A compiler-proven callable identifier is a safe Solid 2 apply function. This control prevents conservative handling of `any`, assertions, bundles, and spreads from turning every non-literal argument into an uncertifiable finding.

SC4004 is independent, and it is the consumer that kept the cleanup-return *classification* alive after SC3004 went. Returning a real cleanup from an unowned `onSettled` is perfectly typed; the claim is that nothing will ever dispose it -- an ownership fact.

The callback may legally return either a cleanup or undefined. TypeScript accepts both, while owner safety depends on the runtime branch, so SC4004 must remain an explicit proof obligation rather than treating the cleanup as absent.
A callback that returns a number is already rejected by the published onSettled signature. SC4004 is an ownership rule and must not duplicate that return-type error.
cases.code:
import { onSettled } from "solid-js";
onSettled(() => 1);

cases.why: SC4002 is independent. `onCleanup` takes a `Disposable` and this argument is one; the claim is that no owner is active at the call, which is a runtime ownership fact.
cases.code:
import { onCleanup } from "solid-js";
onCleanup(() => {});

cases.why: SC1002 is independent. Reading an accessor after an `await` is type-correct in every respect; the claim is about when the read happens relative to the tracking scope.

SC1005's three typed value positions, narrowed 2026-08-17: a native JSX attribute (TS2322 -- an accessor is never assignable to a DOM attribute's type), a class object value (TS2322 against 2.0's `Record<string, boolean>`), and a computed property access (TS2538, "cannot be used as an index type"). All three hold in both dialects. The rule SURVIVES on the positions TypeScript permits -- see the sibling `silent` case.

SC1005's surviving positions, and the reason it was narrowed rather than deleted -- these are the most common real spellings of the bug. String concatenation accepts any operand, a unary operator accepts a function, and a template literal stringifies whatever it is given, so TypeScript permits all three while the rendered output is the accessor's own source text and never updates. The native-attribute position survives in one shape for the same reason: TypeScript does not check a hyphenated JSX attribute name, so `data-count={count}` is accepted and the accessor is stringified into the attribute with nothing to say so.
Binary arithmetic and bitwise operators reject a function operand -- TS2365 for `+`, TS2362 for `-`, `*`, and `|` -- so those positions are TypeScript-owned and SC1005 must not duplicate them.

TypeScript accepts a function operand for the unary numeric coercions: `-f`, `+f`, and `~f` are all clean against the published typings in both passes. An accessor coerced there silently becomes NaN, which no type error covers, so it is this checker's to report.
Reading an accessor is type-correct wherever it happens; the claim is that this read registers no dependency because of the scope it runs in. No type describes a tracking scope.

SC1001's keystone. Reading an accessor in a component body is an ordinary call returning `number`, so TypeScript is satisfied. The claim is that the body runs once: the read sees the current value and never updates when `count` changes. No type distinguishes a read that will re-run from one that will not, which is why the sibling case -- minimal enough that the owner rules answer first -- could not carry this.
A derived helper and its call are both well typed; the claim is that the call site is outside any tracking scope, so the derivation is frozen.

SC1006's keystone. `doubled` is an ordinary function and calling it is an ordinary call, so nothing here is a type error. The claim is that every call to it is untracked, so its reads subscribe to nothing and the derivation never updates -- a fact about which scopes track, which the type system does not model.

SC2003's surviving store arms in 2.0, each a write TypeScript accepts while the runtime drops it. The cast is the one that constrains the implementation: `member_root` resolves through it, so the narrowing must require the written member's object to be a bare *identifier* rather than merely equal to the resolved root span. The capitalized ordinary helper with no JSX result is a negative control: its parameter is not component props merely because the function is named `Props`.

TypeScript accepts both accessor arguments, but policy 2 retires the old policy-1 receipt that claimed `@solidjs/signals@2.0.0-rc.3` `isEqual` was inert. Until that exact artifact is recertified with authenticated policy-2 witnesses, each reactive source crossing the now-obsolete package boundary remains independently uncertifiable.

The function is declared through the real published `@solidjs/web` type surface but its implementation is deliberately outside this project and no package contract is attached to the ambient binding. Passing a proven Solid accessor to that opaque boundary remains a correct uncertifiable obligation; this preserves a positive keystone without treating the partially audited `@solidjs/signals` package as if its unmodeled exports were known.
Destructuring a props object is ordinary TypeScript; the claim is that the properties are lazy getters, so the bindings freeze at setup.
Both branches return valid JSX; the claim is that a component body runs once, so whichever branch is taken at setup renders forever.

Calling a JSX-returning function is a plain call and type checks, so TypeScript is silent. The checker is silent here too, and by design: SC8018's subject is a *lowercase* JSX-returning function, whose documented remedy is to rename it and call it as a component (docs/rules/prefer-component-syntax.md). A capitalized callee is already component-named, so the rename the rule asks for does not apply and it is out of scope. The sibling case carries the lowercase spelling the rule does report.

SC8018's keystone. Calling a JSX-returning function with the right argument types checks exactly as written. The claim is that the imperative call hides component identity and can evaluate setup logic in the caller's reactive expression instead of under a component owner of its own. The callee here is lowercase, which is the rule's documented subject: SC8018 asks that a lowercase JSX-returning function be renamed and called as a component. A capitalized callee is already component-named and out of scope, which is what the sibling case records.
Calling a setter is type-correct; the claim is that a write while a children-capable owner is active starts a transaction the runtime refuses.

SC2001's keystone. A setter accepts the value it is given, so the write type checks. The claim is an execution-model one: the write happens under a children-capable owner while that owner is computing, which creates a feedback loop in the reactive graph. Solid itself throws REACTIVE_WRITE_IN_OWNED_SCOPE here in dev -- the clearest evidence the defect is a runtime one and not a typing one.
`onCleanup` takes a `Disposable` and receives one; the claim is that a leaf owner has no scope to register disposal on, so the call throws.

SC3001's keystone. `onCleanup` accepts the callback it is handed, so TypeScript says nothing. The claim is about which owner the registration lands on: `createTrackedEffect` is a leaf owner that manages cleanup through its return value instead, and Solid throws CLEANUP_IN_FORBIDDEN_SCOPE here in dev. A leaf owner is the shape the sibling case was missing -- at module scope the owner rules answer first.
cases.code:
import { createTrackedEffect, onCleanup } from "solid-js";
createTrackedEffect(() => onCleanup(() => {}));

cases.why: Creating a memo is well typed anywhere; the claim is that a leaf owner cannot own the computation, so it leaks or throws.

SC3002's keystone. Creating a memo inside a callback is well typed wherever the callback sits. The claim is that `createTrackedEffect` is a leaf owner with no children, so a primitive created under it is never tracked or disposed, and Solid throws in dev. Ownership shape is not something a type carries.
cases.code:
import { createTrackedEffect, createMemo } from "solid-js";
createTrackedEffect(() => createMemo(() => 1));

cases.why: `flush()` takes no arguments and returns void; the claim is about the phase it is called in.

SC3003's keystone. `flush()` takes no arguments and returns nothing, so no call site of it is a type error. The claim is about execution phase: a tracked effect runs as part of the flush cycle, so the call re-enters the scheduler, and Solid throws here in dev. Phase is exactly what the type system does not track.
cases.code:
import { createTrackedEffect, flush } from "solid-js";
createTrackedEffect(() => flush());

cases.why: A module-scope effect with a compiler-proven callable apply function is a well typed call; the claim is that no owner exists to dispose it, which is a runtime ownership fact. The named callback is deliberate: this pins that conservative handling of `any` and assertions does not weaken ordinary typed identifiers into uncertainty.
The call type-checks; the claim is that the boundary it needs is not established at this point in the ownership graph.

SC4003's keystone. A boundary element at module scope is perfectly well typed -- it is just an element. The claim is an ownership one: created with no reactive owner above it, the boundary can never be disposed, and the subtree it manages leaks for the lifetime of the app.
cases.code:
import { Loading } from "solid-js";
export const Orphan = <Loading>{null}</Loading>;

cases.why: Calling an action is a well typed call; the claim is that it starts a write transaction while a children-capable owner is active.

SC2002's keystone. Calling an action is an ordinary call of a well typed value. The claim is that invoking one starts a write transaction -- optimistic writes, refresh -- under a children-capable owner, which re-triggers the very scope that called it. A transaction's interaction with the owner tree is not expressible as a type.
`resolve` returns a Promise and is called correctly; the claim is that the runtime's observer guard throws when it runs directly in a tracked scope.
cases.code:
import { createMemo, resolve } from "solid-js";
export const value = createMemo(() => resolve(() => 1));

cases.why: 2.0's `ComputeFunction` admits `PromiseLike<Next>`, so an async compute type-checks; the claim is about which node kind can carry an async computation.

SC7002's keystone. `{ sync: true }` is a declared option and an `async` computation is a legal computation, so the two compose without complaint. The claim is that `sync: true` asserts a synchronous result so the runtime may skip the async-shape probe: dev still probes and throws SYNC_NODE_RECEIVED_ASYNC, and production stores the unawaited value as-is. The contradiction is between an option's runtime meaning and the callback's shape, which no signature relates.
The async compute and the read are both well typed; the claim is about the pending state a read observes after the await.

SC5001's keystone. Reading the accessor and taking a property off the result is well typed throughout. The claim is that a pending async accessor read outside a tracking scope cannot suspend or retry, so there is nothing to await on and Solid throws PENDING_ASYNC_UNTRACKED_READ in dev. Whether the surrounding scope tracks is not part of the accessor's type.
Rendering an async computation's value is type-correct; the claim is that no `<Loading>` boundary encloses the read, which is a tree-position fact.

SC2003's root-record arm, narrowed 2026-08-17 in the 2.0 catalog only. `createStore` returns a shallowly `Readonly` proxy there, so a write to a root property is TS2540 for both the assignment and the update form. Solid 1.x is the opposite -- its store type is mutable throughout and the same writes produce no diagnostic at all -- so the 1.x rule is untouched, which is why the predicate is asked of the dialect. The rule SURVIVES on nested records, casts, and props members; see the sibling `silent` case.
A callable prop is a legal Solid 2 event handler, while the finding says reading the prop during setup freezes which handler was installed and loses later reactive replacement.
cases.code:
const Comp = (props: { onSave: () => void }) => <button onClick={props.onSave} />;
export default Comp;

cases.why: Solid 2's published EnumeratedPseudoBoolean type rejects both JSX shorthand and draggable={true} with TS2322, so those presence-only runtime spellings are TypeScript-owned. The rule survives on well-typed draggable={false} for default-draggable elements.

cases.why: Solid 2 types accept draggable={false}, but the renderer removes the attribute; on an image that selects HTML's auto state and silently re-enables default dragging.
cases.code: export const Case = () => ;

cases.why: For an anchor, auto-dragging depends on whether href remains present. A dynamic href may be removed when nullish, and a later spread may overwrite a static href; both outcomes are possible, so the checker must preserve an obligation without claiming a violation.
A spread before a later static href cannot remove that final href. The anchor is therefore proven draggable in auto state after Solid removes draggable={false}.
cases.code: declare const earlier: { href?: string }; export const Case = () => open;

cases.why: An anchor with neither an href attribute nor a spread is proven non-draggable in the HTML auto state, so removing draggable={false} preserves the requested behavior.
cases.code: export const Case = () => label;

cases.why: Creating a reactive primitive while a directive is applied is type-correct in Solid 2; the finding is about compiler execution phase and the directive application's leaf ownership.

A function-level use-server directive is only a framework convention: the source alone does not prove whether a transform selects Solid 2's server entry. The one-argument call is a client defect but inert on the server, so the checker must preserve the unresolved execution mode as uncertifiable rather than certify or assert a violation.

The directive does not prove whether the client or server entry executes. The two-argument createEffect, createRenderEffect, and createTrackedEffect allocate owner-bound computations on the client but not on the server; each must therefore be an uncertifiable ownership obligation. The one-argument createEffect allocates under neither possible path and stays silent.

A spread hides whether createEffect receives the deprecated one-argument form that throws before allocation or the two-argument form that allocates an owner-bound computation. At module scope the ownership claim is therefore uncertifiable, not a proven violation and not safe silence.

Both calls are accepted by the published signature, but neither proves that the runtime value reaches allocation: `any` may be undefined, and a non-null assertion does not change a nullable value. The owner obligation must remain explicit without being promoted to a violation. A separate named-callback keystone pins the ordinary proven path.

The undirected control for the server-entry uncertainty case: the identical three constructors without the directive. Every call is well typed -- TypeScript has nothing to say about where an effect is created -- and each allocates a computation at module scope that no owner will dispose. If the server-entry uncertainty ever widens past the directive, these three go silent and this case fails.

Both object implementations satisfy the same TypeScript interface, but one reads a signal and the other is inert. TypeScript deliberately does not express reactive-read behavior, so the runtime union must remain an explicit proof obligation rather than being narrowed to either candidate.
Calling a computed numeric element is already TS2349. SC9012 requires a TypeScript-valid call and must not duplicate that invalid-call diagnostic merely because the runtime target is unresolved.

The published API accepts the wrapper result as a leaf callback, but the wrapper decides what function actually reaches createTrackedEffect. A specific forbidden operation is not proven and safety is not proven, so the leaf path must remain explicit as SC9012.

The server function's declared Date parameter makes the call type-correct, but the default client transport rejects Date at runtime. The finding is therefore about transport behavior that the published TypeScript signature does not express.

The object argument is well typed, but its nested Date makes the default transport reject it. JSON.stringify reaches nested values, and this literal is closed -- no spread, no computed key, distinct keys -- so the nested library identity proves the flattening rather than leaving an obligation. TypeScript stays silent because the declared parameter type is satisfied; the defect is transport behavior the signature does not express.
The compiler proves the alias contains only strings, booleans, null, and finite numeric literals. Those values are all faithfully JSON-serializable, so no transport obligation remains.

Bigint, symbol, and undefined are accepted by the declared parameter type, but the compiler proves that each call passes a primitive the default JSON transport cannot encode faithfully. These are transport violations, not TypeScript diagnostics.

Type assertions change only TypeScript's apparent type. The runtime bigint still fails the default JSON transport and must report, while the runtime number asserted to bigint remains JSON-safe and must stay silent.
A broad number type may contain finite JSON numbers or non-finite values such as NaN and Infinity. Without an exact finite-value guarantee, the checker must retain the transport obligation.

The extra rich argument is already rejected by TS2554. SC7007 now requires a compiler-valid call and must not add a transport finding to code that cannot satisfy the declared server-function signature.

SC5005's keystone. The source option and JSX read are well typed; the finding combines the runtime meaning of ssrSource: client, the absence of a Loading ancestor, and a project-level server-rendering entry.

The same well-typed client-hole shape without a visible server entry cannot be certified safe: the entry may live in another tsconfig or package. The checker must expose that project-boundary uncertainty.
SC7005's keystone. Calling httpStatus is well typed; the finding is about render-tree dominance and whether a streaming shell may commit before the Loading child settles.
The same well-typed dominated response write without a visible server entry cannot be certified as a CSR no-op because the server entry may be analyzed elsewhere.
The Solid 2 project has the same TypeScript JSX exemption and native on-prefixed listener lowering. A numeric runtime value is proven not to be either a function or an array-backed bound handler.
cases.code:
const handler = 1;
export const Case = () => <button on-event={handler}>save</button>;

cases.why: The native listener position is unchecked by TypeScript and its union can be callable or non-callable. Reporting a violation would guess, while silence would certify it, so Solid 2 retains the same explicit obligation.
cases.code:
declare const handler: (() => void) | number;
export const Case = () => <button on-event={handler}>save</button>;

cases.why: Solid 2 likewise certifies a directly callable handler on the unchecked custom event spelling; only invalid or unresolved runtime shapes are reported.
cases.code:
const handler = () => {};
export const Case = () => <button on-event={handler}>save</button>;

cases.why: A directly rendered Array#map is valid TypeScript; the finding recommends Solid 2 list identity semantics that the type system cannot express.
A logical JSX branch is valid TypeScript; the finding is an opt-in control-flow preference and does not claim a type defect.
Solid 2.0's published JSX child types accept this async mapped array. The opt-in finding still expresses list identity rather than a type defect, but withholds its synchronous-callback autofix.
The published Solid 2 typings type innerHTML and children independently, while the DOM runtime gives them one competing content slot.
